sources.entry: Simple, Fast, and Practical Non-Blocking and Blocking Concurrent Queue Algorithms - The lock-free queue later libraries copy, with the counted pointer against ABA and a two-lock queue beside it.

summary.title: Simple, Fast, and Practical Non-Blocking and Blocking Concurrent Queue Algorithms
summary.one_liner: A 1996 PODC paper by Michael and Scott presenting a lock-free compare-and-swap FIFO queue with modification counters against ABA, and a two-lock queue with separate head and tail locks, both benchmarked on a 12-node SGI Challenge.
keywords: concurrent fifo queue in plain english
how to build a thread-safe queue without locks
takeaways: The non-blocking queue uses a singly-linked list with Head and Tail pointers and a dummy node, updated via compare-and-swap.
Modification counters paired with pointers are used to mitigate the ABA problem, which the paper notes makes it extremely unlikely rather than impossible.
The two-lock queue lets one enqueue and one dequeue proceed concurrently, with the dummy node preventing lock-ordering deadlock.
Experiments on a 12-processor SGI Challenge show the lock-free queue outperforming alternatives, and the two-lock queue beating a single lock under contention.
The paper reviews prior queue designs (Valois, Prakash et al., Stone, Mellor-Crummey) and their races, memory-reuse, or blocking problems.
summary.summary: The paper presents two concurrent FIFO queue algorithms: a non-blocking queue built on compare-and-swap with modification counters to handle ABA, and a two-lock queue with separate Head and Tail locks. Both are given as commented pseudo-code (Figures 1 and 2), followed by safety, linearizability, and liveness arguments. Section 4 benchmarks them on a 12-processor SGI Challenge against a single-lock queue and several prior algorithms, under both dedicated and multiprogrammed workloads. The related-work discussion is also a useful survey of earlier lock-free queue designs and their flaws.
